title: HOSEA MARRIED GOMER—AND THEN GOD GAVE THEIR CHILDREN NAMES NO PARENT WOULD EVER WANT TO CALL ACROSS THE HOUSE
paragraphs: HOSEA MARRIED GOMER—AND THEN GOD GAVE THEIR CHILDREN NAMES NO PARENT WOULD EVER WANT TO CALL ACROSS THE HOUSE

Jezreel. Lo-Ruhamah. Lo-Ammi. Three children. Three devastating names. But buried inside those names of judgment was a promise that reaches all the way to Jesus Christ—and perhaps straight into the part of your life you thought God could never redeem.
Imagine holding your newborn child for the first time.
A face that has never seen betrayal, war, shame, rejection, or grief.
Then God tells you what to name the child.
And by the third child, the name itself sounds almost unbearable:
This is where the book of Hosea begins.
And, astonishingly, with grace already moving beneath the wreckage.
Because if you stop reading Hosea when the judgment falls, you will misunderstand Hosea.
And if you stop reading the story of your own life at your worst chapter, you may misunderstand what the grace of God can do too.

Hosea ministered during the eighth century before Christ, during the reigns named in the opening verse of the book. Israel could still look prosperous from the outside, but spiritually something was rotting underneath.
God's covenant people were running after other gods.
They had learned the terrifying art of appearing religious while giving their hearts elsewhere.
And before we point at ancient Israel, perhaps we should recognize how modern that sounds.
You can sing worship songs and still worship approval.
You can carry a Bible and secretly bow to money.
You can post Scripture and be consumed by lust.
You can speak about Jesus while being addicted to applause.
You can sit in church while resentment eats through your heart.
You can know Christian vocabulary without living in surrender to Christ.
Israel's deepest problem was not simply that they had broken religious regulations.
So God gave Hosea a calling that would make the prophet's own home into a living message.
The Hebrew of Hosea 1:2 is deliberately disturbing:
“Go, take for yourself a wife of whoredom/promiscuity.”
Translations differ in how they render the difficult expression אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים — eshet zenunim, but the theological explanation immediately follows:
“For the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD.”
Hosea's marriage becomes a prophetic sign of something much larger.
Israel has been unfaithful to the God who loved her.
“So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim.”
And we should be careful here.

People sometimes tell Gomer's story with details Scripture itself never gives us. Hosea does not provide a modern biography explaining every stage of her life, every motive, or every circumstance surrounding the marriage. Even interpreters have debated precisely how Hosea 1 should be understood.
So we should not pretend to know what God chose not to tell us.
What Scripture makes unmistakable is the prophetic meaning:
Gomer and Hosea's household became a living picture of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness and God's response to it.
The name is connected with the Hebrew idea of God sowing or scattering seed.
But at this moment in Hosea, Jezreel carried blood-soaked historical associations.
God declares judgment concerning the bloodshed of Jezreel and announces that the kingdom of Israel will be brought to an end.
Imagine Hosea calling the boy home.
The child himself has become a sermon walking through the neighborhood.
God's patience must never be confused with moral indifference.
That truth makes many modern ears uncomfortable because we prefer a God who comforts but never confronts.
But biblical grace cannot be understood apart from biblical holiness.
The God who forgives sin is the same God who calls sin what it is.
If sin were merely an insignificant mistake, Calvary would make no sense.
Jesus did not die because sin was trivial.
He died because sin was deadly.
And God gave her an even more painful name:
The Hebrew word רָחַם — racham carries the idea of compassion, mercy, or tender pity.
Put לֹא — lo, meaning “not,” before it and the name becomes devastating:
Different English translations express the nuance differently, but the blow is unmistakable.
Imagine hearing your name spoken every morning.
Every time someone called her, Israel was hearing a warning.
There comes a point when persistent rebellion encounters judgment.
This was not because God had suddenly become cruel.
The tragedy of Hosea is precisely the opposite.
Israel was rejecting the God whose covenant love had sustained her.
It was self-destruction dressed as freedom.
And maybe somebody reading this understands that more personally than you want to admit.
You thought the affair would make you feel alive.
You thought pornography would remain private.
It started rewriting the way you saw people.
You thought bitterness was protecting you.
You thought money would quiet the insecurity.
You simply became afraid of losing more.
You thought walking away from God would finally make you free.
But at 2:17 in the morning, when nobody is watching and the noise is gone, something inside you still knows:
You were created for more than this.
Then there are chains we discover afterward.
And God loves us too deeply to call chains freedom.
This time the name cuts even deeper:
The covenant relationship itself is now being invoked.
It is difficult to imagine a heavier name.
Lo-Ruhamah spoke withdrawn compassion in the face of persistent rebellion.
And this is where someone carrying shame may begin to hear the wrong sermon.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Maybe your family thinks you're fine.
Your church friends think you're fine.
And somewhere along the way, you stopped merely saying, “I did something shameful.”
That is one of Satan's favorite distortions.
Condemnation says, “Hide because there is no way home.”
But Hosea refuses to end where shame expects it to end.
Because immediately after the terrifying words “Not My People,” something happens.
The same chapter that announces judgment suddenly declares that Israel's number will again be immeasurable and that in the very place where it had been said,
The location of rejection becomes the location where restoration is announced.
The place associated with judgment becomes the place where grace speaks another word.
“I will say to Lo-Ammi, ‘You are My people.’”
The one called “No Mercy” receives mercy.
The one called “Not My People” hears:
This does not mean judgment was imaginary.
It means judgment was not the final word in God's redemptive purpose.
Biblical grace never says sin did not matter.
Biblical grace says sin mattered so much that redemption cost blood.
And centuries after Hosea carried this painful prophetic message, another Son would enter the story of Israel.
He would not merely act out a prophetic sign.
He would fulfill God's saving purpose.
And then He would walk toward a cross.
There the scandal becomes almost incomprehensible.
The sinless One bears the sins of sinners.
The Son of God gives Himself for people who have not loved God faithfully.
The New Testament describes it with breathtaking clarity:
Romans 5 places this death in the context of God's love toward sinners.
Not people who had finally made themselves respectable.
Not bad people becoming impressive enough for God.
Not broken people repairing themselves until heaven approves the workmanship.
Not religious people accumulating enough spiritual points.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
And this is why Hosea's painful names cannot be reduced to an inspirational message about “believing in yourself.”
Hosea is not telling you that you were secretly wonderful all along.
The Gospel tells something far better.
You were more lost than self-help can repair…
and more deeply loved in Christ than shame wants you to believe.
Grace takes guilty people who come to Christ and gives them something they could never earn.
The apostle Peter later reaches directly into Hosea's language when speaking about God's people:
“Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.”
That is Hosea's language echoing inside the Gospel age.
Not because everybody automatically belongs to God regardless of repentance and faith.
But because God's mercy creates a people who belong to Him.
And that means your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Your adultery does not have to write the last sentence.
Your addiction does not have to write the last sentence.
Your pride does not have to write the last sentence.
Your secret life does not have to write the last sentence.
Your church hurt does not have to write the last sentence.
Your failure as a parent does not have to write the last sentence.
Your wasted years do not have to write the last sentence.
Your shame does not get editorial control over eternity.
Grace is not permission to remain where grace found you.
Jesus does not merely forgive us so that we can decorate our chains with Christian language.
Repentance is not paying God back for mercy.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has finally stopped defending the thing that is destroying it.
Maybe that is what God is doing with you right now.
Maybe the reason this article feels uncomfortable is not because God hates you.
Maybe His Word is putting its finger on something you have spent months protecting.
The blood of Jesus is not reserved for people with respectable testimonies.
And Christians never graduate from needing grace.
Some of us simply become better at hiding how badly we need it.
If you need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply write:
And if Christ has already carried you through a season that should have destroyed you, don't hide the testimony either.
Someone scrolling through those comments may need to discover that Christians are not a museum of flawless people.
We are people who desperately need a Savior.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
But if God's truth has helped you, sharing it can put that truth in front of someone you may never know is struggling.
Someone's smiling profile picture may be hiding a collapsing marriage.
Someone posting jokes may be fighting despair.
Someone who has not entered a church for fifteen years may still stop long enough to read about Hosea.
Someone convinced that God could never want them again may discover that the Bible contains a story where “Not My People” is followed by the astonishing promise:
More importantly, we want this community to become something deeper than content people consume for a moment and forget.
And continual reminders that everything eventually has to lead back to Jesus Christ.
Because there may come a night when you need these three names again.
You may need to remember that Scripture does not sentimentalize rebellion.
But you may also need to remember what happened afterward.
“Not My People” was answered with “You are My people.”
And the story eventually leads us toward the One whose wounds tell guilty sinners that grace is not imaginary.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the friend quietly fighting addiction.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is only for respectable people.
Invite the skeptic willing to listen.
Invite the prodigal who still remembers the sound of worship songs from childhood.
And yes, invite the person whose life looks like a scandal right now.
Because Christianity began spreading through a world full of people with complicated histories.
And Christ is still saving people like us.
Hosea carried children whose names announced judgment through the streets of Israel.
But God did not allow those names to be the end of the story.
That is the breathtaking tension of Hosea.
And eventually, for everyone who belongs to Christ, shame loses the right to introduce you by the name of the person you used to be.
Maybe people know what you did.
Jesus knows what His blood can do.
Maybe someone has permanently attached a label to your name.
Jesus Christ is not intimidated by labels.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Make restitution where righteousness requires it.
Seek forgiveness where you wounded someone.
Stop asking darkness to give you what only Christ can give.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Hosea's children is not simply that they received names of judgment.
It is that God deliberately returned to those very names and spoke restoration over them.
The wound became the location where mercy was announced.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this was meant to carry into tonight:
The name your failure gave you does not have to be the name grace leaves you with.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody still believes their scandal is the end of their story.
Maybe your share is how they encounter the message that it isn't.
Maybe your testimony is how they discover they are not alone.
Maybe the truth you almost scrolled past becomes the truth God uses to turn somebody's eyes back toward Jesus.
And long after they forget who shared the article, may they remember the Savior it pointed them toward.
Judgment may expose the name sin gave us—but at the cross, grace shows us what it cost for Jesus to call His people home.
